articles.title: In 2023, Parliament bell ringer tore out gate to banker neighbour’s £2 million Fulham home; High Court now orders him to sell his £1 million London house after failing to pay £129,500 in damages and costs
articles.summary: UK News: A veteran Parliament bell ringer has been ordered to give up his £1 million London home after failing to pay more than £100,000 owed to neighbours fol.
articles.body: A veteran Parliament bell ringer has been ordered to give up his £1 million London home after failing to pay more than £100,000 owed to neighbours following a bitter dispute over the entrance to their £2 million property. The details were reported by the Daily Mail.Adrian Udal, 66, became embroiled in the legal battle after he removed a roller gate and door belonging to financier Nicholas Patrick-Hiley’s mews home in Fulham, west London, in August 2023.Patrick-Hiley had just completed the purchase of the property and arrived at his new home to find Udal and another man dismantling the gates.Dispute over access to £2 million homeThe Patrick-Hileys had planned to turn the property into their retirement home. However, the dispute with their neighbour soon escalated into a lengthy legal battle.Udal argued that he was entitled to remove the gate because he owned the land on which it stood. The Patrick-Hileys challenged that position in court and won their case last year.Judge Nicholas Parfitt described Udal’s actions as a “carefully pre-planned” act of “wanton destruction”.Udal was ordered to pay the couple £10,000 in damages in June 2025 and was later ordered to cover £85,000 in their legal costs, excluding his own expenses. With interest and further costs, the amount owed had grown considerably.Court orders sale of Udal’s homeAt the latest High Court hearing, Deputy Master Martin Dray was told that Udal had not paid any of the money awarded against him and had indicated that he had no intention of doing so.“The claimants are out of pocket and owed a considerable amount of money, which is ever increasing,” the judge said.“The defendant has made no attempt to repay any part of it... quite the contrary, he has disclaimed any liability to pay one penny piece.”The court subsequently granted the Patrick-Hileys possession and sale orders, allowing them to recover the debt by selling Udal’s property.The original judgment debt is understood to be around £104,500, while Udal was ordered to pay a further £25,000 in costs related to the latest hearing.Udal has 28 days to hand over propertyUdal has been given 28 days to surrender possession of his home. However, the order will not be enforced if he settles the outstanding amount before October 2.The judge noted that Udal had not participated in the proceedings concerning the proposed sale of his house. He nevertheless ruled that the case could not be allowed to “derail”.The decision came after an earlier “frosty conversation” between the neighbours following Christmas, during which Udal allegedly made clear that he did not intend to make any payments. He had also already lost an attempt to appeal the original ruling.Who is Adrian Udal?Udal is a veteran bell ringer who has worked in connection with special church, state and parliamentary occasions. He has also spoken of his pride in having “rung in” the New Year almost every year since 2000.In 2021, he became secretary of the belfry at St Margaret’s Church beside Westminster Abbey. The historic church serves as a place of worship for Parliament.Patrick-Hiley, meanwhile, is a retired financier who previously served as managing director and head of sales for North America at investment banking firm Panmure Gordon.Unusual layout at centre of disputeThe neighbouring properties have an unusual arrangement. Patrick-Hiley’s house sits behind Udal’s property and can be reached via a drive and passageway running beneath part of Udal’s home before opening into the couple’s courtyard.While Udal owns the drive and passageway, the Patrick-Hileys have rights allowing them to use the route to access their home.The couple had known about an earlier disagreement involving the previous owner of their property and Udal. They nevertheless approached him after buying the house and offered him an opportunity to contribute to plans for “better looking and more functional gates”.The situation appeared settled until Udal was allegedly seen removing the existing fixtures and preparing to install metal barriers of his own. He had reportedly purchased the barriers about a month earlier.Udal maintained that he was exercising his rights as freeholder. However, Judge Parfitt rejected his argument and criticised his evidence during the original proceedings, describing him as a “poor witness” who appeared to favour his own interpretation of events over the objective facts.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Pro-life vs socialism: GOP lawmakers divided over controversial guaranteed income programs
articles.summary: The Mother & Infant Cash Coalition says conservative lawmakers are backing direct cash transfers for mothers and newborns on pro-family grounds.
articles.body: Although guaranteed income programs have faced partisan pushback nationwide since gaining national traction in 2018, a growing faction of conservatives is finding common ground with direct cash initiatives centered on mothers and newborns. According to Tegan Lecheler, national program director for the Mother and Infant Cash Coalition (MICC), the "common-sense" nature of early childhood cash transfers has prompted conservative lawmakers and advocates to reach out to her organization in support. "I think we're in a really polarized time politically right now," Lecheler told Fox News Digital. "We are not a political organization and want to work to improve families' outcomes. We believe an effective strategy for doing that is to build a big tent – a wide tent with a lot of people underneath it." EXCLUSIVE: PENCE GROUP KNOCKS VANCE PLAN TO PAY STAY-AT-HOME PARENTS UP TO $9K PER CHILD Lecheler noted that early childhood support aligns with pro-family conservative principles. "Some of the solutions that we're putting forward really resonate with have been folks who agree that people should be able to have families that look the way they want," Lecheler said. "There are certain factions that are excited by the idea of cash transfers specifically within the period surrounding the birth of a child because it enables families to have the number of kids that they want to have." Founded in 2023, the Mother and Infant Cash Coalition grew out of a broader movement toward direct financial support for young families. Lecheler, who previously managed operations with The Bridge Project — an unrestricted cash transfer initiative launched in 2021 that operates across 14 red, blue, and purple states — noted that momentum for direct cash assistance built rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic. Advocates and researchers increasingly argue that flexible cash benefits offer a more cost-effective way to improve family stability than traditional, highly restricted in-kind welfare programs. As direct cash initiatives expanded, organizations focused specifically on the perinatal period — from pregnancy through early infancy — began coordinating nationwide. That collaboration formed the Mother and Infant Cash Coalition, which aims to leverage early-childhood cash transfers to strengthen family stability and drive better maternal and child health outcomes. Member organizations include the Magnolia Mother’s Trust (MMT), launched in 2018, which provides selected Black mothers with $1,000 per month in unconditional cash for a full year. Mayors for a Guaranteed Income, a coalition of over 150 mayors, bids to solve the affordability crisis with cash handouts. The coalition is responsible for over 100 pilot programs launched since 2018 and the establishment of the program in Cook County, Illinois, which was the first municipality to expand a guaranteed income program permanently. Despite fierce national pushback against guaranteed basic income (GBI) programs — which opponents often criticize as "lottery socialism" — Lecheler stresses that conservative interest often stems from fiscal pragmatic arguments. "There are other folks who are excited about it from sort of an efficiency angle, and think about this work because it is a lower administrative burden," Lecheler told Fox News Digital. "It is also more cost-effective to prevent poor birth outcomes like low birth weight or preterm birth than it is to respond to them after the fact." MAYORS WANT TO KEEP HANDING OUT FREE CASH AFTER FEDERAL FUNDS DRIED UP GOP Divided Over 'Rx Kids' The debate over early cash aid reached a flashpoint in Michigan over "Rx Kids," a citywide bipartisan initiative providing expectant mothers with a lump-sum payment of $1,500 during pregnancy, followed by $500 per month for up to 12 months post-birth. While Rx Kids is not a member of the Mother and Infant Cash Coalition, it operates on a similar direct-cash model. Michigan House Republicans launched a formal inquiry into the initiative, which has absorbed more than $300 million in combined public and private funding. House Oversight Committee Chairman Rep. Jay DeBoyer, R-Clay Township, criticized the program's lack of oversight, arguing it functions as a "redistribution of wealth" that fails to solve systemic poverty without spending guardrails. However, other Michigan Republicans view the policy through a pro-life lens. State Sen. John Damoose, R-Harbor Springs, publicly broke with critics to endorse the initiative. "Helping moms and babies truly fits into the call of Jesus," Damoose wrote in an op-ed for the Detroit Free Press. "I believe in the sanctity of life. I believe we need to be champions for the unborn. That means more than just calling ourselves ‘pro-life’ — it means doing everything we can to make it easier for expectant moms to choose life. It means being there for families from the very beginning — and offering them the resources they need to thrive." MICHIGAN REPUBLICAN LAWMAKER WARNS GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAMS DO NOT WORK, VOICES OPPOSITION TO STATE POLICY National Legal and Legislative Battlelines Similar policy rifts are playing out nationwide as conservative lawmakers evaluate direct cash policies alongside conservative economic priorities. "We have people from the right that have organically reached out to us to voice support," Lecheler noted, pointing to conservative support for policies like the Federal Child Tax Credit (CTC) and proposals to expand Child Care and Development Fund assistance. A spokesperson for the Economic Securities Project (ESP), an organization that led the creation of more than 100 guaranteed income programs, told Fox News Digital that affordability is a growing issue among Americans, calling for the need of direct cash. "Cash assistance is widely supported across party lines, and we see that with the proliferation of cash proposals at the federal level, continued support for different versions of the CTC, as well as promising pilots like Rx Kids and the ASCEND program in New Mexico," Shafeka Hashash, director of Cash Initiatives at Economic Security Project (ESP), told Fox News Digital. "Growing concerns about the cost-of-living crisis and how AI will impact the workforce are also driving bipartisan support for cash." IOWA SUPERVISOR SLAMS BAN ON GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAMS AS STATE ‘WAGING IDEOLOGICAL WARS’ Nevertheless, major state-level legal and legislative efforts to restrict or eliminate cash transfer programs continue in red states: As of 2026, four red states — Arkansas, Idaho, Iowa, and South Dakota — have enacted laws banning or restricting local guaranteed income and unconditional cash-aid programs. In addition, Kansas passed similar restrictive legislation when a bill became law without the governor's signature. To date, Cook County remains the primary local municipality to enact a permanent guaranteed basic income program. For advocates like Lecheler, the policy push comes down to basic economic survival for young families. articles.title: Germany receives first F-35 jet from US as NATO boosts military spending
articles.summary: Germany received the first of nearly three dozen F-35 stealth warplanes it ordered four years ago from Lockheed Martin.
articles.body:
Germany has received its first F-35A Lightning II fighter jet, as the country accelerates a major military buildup and increases defence spending amid a broader push by European NATO members to strengthen their armed forces.

The delivery on Friday is part of Germany’s effort to fulfil NATO nuclear-sharing duties and modernise its military after decades of relatively low defence spending.

Lockheed Martin formally presented the aircraft to the German government during a ceremony at its production facility in Fort Worth, Texas, attended by German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius.

“This is the beginning of a new era for the German Air Force: the new F-35A fighter jet is the world’s most advanced combat aircraft,” Pistorius said in a statement. “It is characterised by its stealth capabilities, close integration with other platforms, and exceptionally powerful sensor technology.”

Germany ordered 35 F-35As in 2022, the year Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine. The aircraft are intended to replace Germany’s ageing Tornado fleet.

The Trump administration has long pressured Europe to spend more on defence, allowing Washington to focus on other challenges such as countering China.

European countries, including Germany, are ramping up military budgets as a result, agreeing in 2025 to Trump’s demand to devote five percent of GDP to security-related spending by 2035.

articles.title: Trump: US strikes security deal with Greenland, Denmark
articles.summary: President Trump said Friday that the United States has entered a security agreement with Greenland and Denmark that gives America a bigger say in the Arctic territory’s affairs and expands its military presence in the country. Trump said the deal “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely…
articles.body:
President Trump said Friday that the United States has entered a security agreement with Greenland and Denmark that gives America a bigger say in the Arctic territory’s affairs and expands its military presence in the country.

Trump said the deal “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns.”

“Additionally, from now on, no U.S. adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval,” he added in a post online .

The Hill is seeking comment from officials representing Greenland and Denmark, which owns the independently governed island.

Trump infuriated Greenland and its allies in NATO with demands for U.S. ownership of the island earlier this year. The deal outlined by Trump appears to fall short of that desire.

The president has argued that greater U.S. control of the island is necessary to ensure it doesn’t fall into the hands of China or Russia amid growing competition over the Arctic.

“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many,” Trump wrote in his post. “We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction.”

A State Department official said the deal “completely and permanently” satisfies all U.S. demands surrounding the Arctic island.

Greenland and Denmark issued a joint statement Friday saying an agreement with the U.S. is expected to be signed next week during the high-level summit of the United Nations General Assembly.

Greenland’s and Denmark’s parliaments will also have to approve the agreement, the statement read.

“It is gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance,” Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said.

“The agreement recognizes Greenland’s interests and our place in international cooperation. It is to the benefit of us all.”

Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the agreement “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination.”

In a later post to the social platform X on Friday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reiterated Trump’s assertion that the U.S. military would immediately begin to develop “a large military presence” in Greenland, referring to the U.S. Northern Command — the military arm that oversees operation in North America.

articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Friday announced an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that he said gives the United States permanent control over security and other security-related needs on the Arctic island.Trump said the agreement would give Washington the ability to act in Greenland to protect US and Greenlandic security, while also preventing US adversaries from establishing military bases or making sensitive investments on the island without American approval. Meanwhile, the 'sovereignity' stays with the Denmark.“I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many US concerns,” Trump said.“There will be no cost to the United States!” he added.Trump further said the agreement would ensure that Washington could act whenever necessary to protect Greenland and the US. “At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will forever have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America,” he said.Under the arrangement, Trump said, "from now on, no US adversary can ever have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval,” Trump said.He also announced plans for a larger US military presence on the island. “We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many,” Trump said, adding, “We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction.”Trump described the agreement as permanent and said it addressed a strategic issue that he argued previous US presidents had failed to resolve. “This is an ‘Infinite Life’ Agreement, there is no end!” he said.“For over 100 years, Presidents have known the strategic importance of Greenland, but none of them were able to do anything about it. I am proud to be the President that permanently and conclusively addressed this very important situation,” Trump added.Trump said the agreement would benefit the United States, Denmark, Greenland and US allies. “This solution is a great one for the United States of America, Denmark, Greenland, and all of our Allies,” he said.Greenland, Denmark issued a statement saying they expect to sign deal with the US on the sidelines of UN General Assembly. Denmark's prime minister described the deal as "good for NATO and Europe". Mette Frederiksen added that the deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area". Shefurther said “the agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity” of Greenland and Denmark and upholds both people's right "to self-determination.”Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, has been at the centre of a major diplomatic dispute since Trump repeatedly demanded that the United States take control of the strategically located Arctic island. Denmark and Greenland had rejected those demands in the past, while Trump has cited US national security and growing Russian and Chinese activity in the Arctic as reasons for his push.The United States already maintains a military installation at Pituffik Space Base in Greenland under its defence arrangements with Denmark. Trump’s latest announcement would significantly expand Washington’s stated military and security role on the island.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: “Wrong again”: Andrew Kolvet hits back at Candace Owens over claims about Erika Kirk’s Idaho event
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Candace Owens and Turning Point USA are clashing over a Club America event at Nampa Christian School in Idaho. Owens alleged that 500 students were re.
articles.body: Candace Owens and Turning Point USA are clashing over a Club America event at Nampa Christian School in Idaho. Owens alleged that 500 students were required to attend the event featuring Erika Kirk and said parents were not allowed to join them. TPUSA spokesperson Andrew Kolvet rejected the claim and said students could opt out. He said three students did so while 500 chose to attend. The disagreement then shifted to whether students had voluntarily signed up for the event or whether the school organized it as part of the regular school day at all.Candace Owens questions whether Nampa Christian students chose to attend Erika Kirk eventThe dispute began after a post about the Club America tour stop celebrated the attendance of more than 500 students at Nampa Christian School. The post described Erika Kirk as delivering a message to a new generation of “America First leaders.” Owens responded by saying she had received emails from parents about the event.Owens described it as a “secret” gathering and claimed it was being held during the school day for middle and high school students. She questioned why a political organization was addressing minors at a private Christian school.Her main concern then became whether students had willingly signed up to attend.In one X post, Owens wrote:“The students were forced to attend this event as a school assembly. They could not opt out. The parents were informed they were not allowed to attend alongside with them.”She also questioned whether the event was being presented as evidence of voluntary interest in Club America when it may have been organized as part of the school's regular schedule.Owens later tagged Andrew Kolvet and argued that Charlie Kirk's original vision for Club America was based on students choosing to join and participate. She said the current event did not fit that model if students were brought to it through a school assembly.Kolvet disputed that description. He said students had the ability to opt out and that three students did so. According to Kolvet, more than 500 students remained at the event by choice.Andrew Kolvet says students could opt out as Owens continues questioningKolvet also explained why the event had not been publicly promoted ahead of time. He said TPUSA does not publicly market some events for security reasons and to maintain a safe environment for students.He also rejected the idea that the event was hidden from parents. Kolvet said parents had been informed and had the option to have their children opt out, and said she is “wrong again.”Owens continued to press him on a different question. She asked whether students had actually signed up for the event themselves or whether the school administration had scheduled it as part of the school day.“You didn’t answer my question. Did the students sign up to attend this event, yes or no? I am aware that technically, you can ‘opt out’ of pretty much anything in High School. But did these students opt-in, Andrew? Or did the administration organize this as a part of their regular day?”Kolvet responded by pointing to the distinction between a school assembly and a regular Club America chapter meeting. He also questioned whether Owens had never attended a school assembly herself.Owens maintained that this did not answer her question. She later said the event was a school assembly and argued that students therefore did not actively opt into it. She also claimed parents received information about the gathering through a weekly newsletter and were told they could not attend.The available public statements establish that the two sides disagree about how attendance should be characterized. Kolvet says students could opt out and that three did. Owens argues that being allowed to opt out is different from voluntarily signing up for an event during the school day.The dispute has also added another public disagreement between Owens and TPUSA leadership. Owens has continued to criticize the direction of the organization and Erika Kirk's role, while TPUSA has rejected her description of the Idaho event.As of September 18, the central disagreement remained unresolved publicly, with neither side providing evidence in the material reviewed that independently establishes whether students were required to attend or voluntarily registered for the event.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump claims deal with Denmark gives US ‘permanent control’ over Greenland
articles.summary: Denmark and Greenland plan to sign a US defence pact next week, pending approval from both parliaments.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump claimed on Friday that Washington has entered into an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that gives the US “permanent control over security and all other needs”.

In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said, “At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the US will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland”.

He added that US adversaries will be barred from establishing military bases or stationing personnel in Greenland unless they receive written authorisation from the US.

Trump said plans will begin immediately to build a significant US military footprint in suitable areas across Greenland, adding that there are numerous potential locations.

Denmark and Greenland released a joint statement on Friday indicating that a pact with the US is set to be signed during next week’s United Nations General Assembly session.

The statement added that the agreement remains subject to parliamentary approval in both Nuuk and Copenhagen.

Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the agreement “recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination”.

Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal with the US “strengthens” the territory’s security.

articles.title: When a beloved tree began withering away, locals suspected a killer in their midst
articles.summary: A neighbourhood’s fight to save a cherished ginkgo pits them against an unlikely foe.
articles.body:
Every summer, Seoul turns a deep green, growing dense and lush under humid skies.

But this year, one tree was visibly suffering.

"Green leaves were falling to the ground, which shouldn't happen at that time of year," recalls Jung, who lives near the streetside ginkgo in Buam-dong, a largely residential neighbourhood in the north of Seoul.

The tree is beloved by locals, who believe it has occupied its spot for more than 100 years. So Jung couldn't ignore what she was seeing. With each passing day, her curiosity turned to concern.

A rotting carpet of familiar fan-shaped leaves soon surrounded the tree, a sight so alarming Jung and her neighbours formed a crew of amateur detectives to solve the mystery: what was ailing their hardy ginkgo?

The whodunnit engrossed Buam-dong and piqued the country's interest, making national headlines. But the attention unsettled Jung, who spearheaded the campaign but has since requested anonymity - we are using a pseudonym.

"Imagine a grandfather who silently embraces you every day, listens to you, and has always been strong and full of life," she says. "Suddenly, he begins to die.

So began one community's fight to save a cherished symbol of their neighbourhood. Their unlikely enemy, who they believe plotted a surreptitious attack, was a museum built to honour a pioneering, nature-loving Korean artist.

Tucked between two mountains, Buam-dong is recommended by travellers and locals for its picturesque views, art galleries and cosy cafes - an escape from Seoul's bustle.

Because of its proximity to the Blue House, the president's official residence, urban development has been restricted, allowing the neighbourhood to retain its quaint charm.

In a place where you usually find ginkgo trees in private gardens or untamed forests, this one is special, Jung says, because it flourished on the side of the road. To her, it's "Grandpa Ginkgo".

"I pass this tree whenever I come home. I would say, 'Grandpa, I'm home.' Or 'Grandpa, I'm heading out now'."

Jung only moved here four years ago, but the grand old tree was the first thing she noticed, and she grew to love it.

"It was the only tree in the neighbourhood that belongs to everyone."

To Park Jeon-hee, who has lived here for nearly all his 74 years, the ginkgo is his "oldest friend".

It's the same for 10-year-old Kim On, who walks past it everyday on his way to school. It has stood since before he was born, Kim says, and "thinking it might fall down makes me sad".

So it wasn't surprising that Jung found ready allies in the community who had also noticed the ginkgo's withering leaves.

They soon became suspicious of 10 white plastic funnels peeping out from behind the trunk. Jung had initially assumed they were providing nutrients, but then began to wonder if something more sinister was at play.

She and her neighbours sieved through security camera footage from a nearby house, until they found something odd: one morning in late April, the camera had recorded two men wearing white gloves and crouching over the base of the tree with a drill.

Were these men installing the funnels? Jung and the others couldn't exactly tell from the footage.

But then they remembered something the local council had told them: a museum had previously asked landowners in the area for permission to remove the tree.

The Whanki Museum had apparently claimed that its outer brick wall, which sits inches from the ginkgo, was under strain from the tree's roots.

The residents soon suspected the funnels contained some kind of herbicide that was slowly killing the tree - a suspicion also shared by arborists who came to examine it. And they believed the Whanki Museum was behind it all.

On the very day they saw the footage, a group of Buam-dong residents stormed into the museum, accompanied by four police officers. When confronted, an employee "basically admitted" the museum had done something to the tree, Jung and her neighbour alleged.

"Once they had said it, there was really no taking it back," the neighbour told the BBC.

The museum has neither publicly confirmed nor denied injecting herbicide into the tree, and has not responded to the BBC's questions.

But it did publish a statement in May, saying the wall of its compound was "collapsing because of the ginkgo's roots". It said it had sent letters to more than 40 property owners "requesting a solution".

There was no response, the museum said, so its staff "attempted to resolve the situation". It did not explain what they had done.

A local council representative told the BBC that an inspection last year found "no meaningful connection" between the ginkgo tree and damage to the museum wall. If there had been an issue, "we would have taken appropriate action and informed the relevant parties," the official added.

The residents, who still believe the Whanki Museum had the funnels installed, want them to reveal what was in them, so experts can treat the ginkgo. They have filed a police report against the museum's director. Officials say police are investigating the case, but police declined to share more information when contacted by the BBC.

Opened in 1992, the museum is dedicated to the late Kim Whanki, a celebrated painter and abstract artist, known by many as the "Picasso of Korea".

On the museum website, architect Woo Kyusung explains he wanted to create a space for Kim's works "that would complement the elements of the nature - the moon, mountains, clouds, rocks and trees - that were so important to his art".

In fact, Kim wrote essays under the pen name Su-wha, which translates to "conversation with trees".

The irony is not lost on Buam-dong's indignant residents. Decades after Kim's death, the museum built in his honour is accused of trying to snuff out a tree. A ginkgo, no less, which is precious in Korea, where it symbolises longevity and resilience.

"Treating life that way is ignorance and there was never any apology," Jung says.

The residents have co-opted Kim's poetic nom de plume "Su-wha" for their moribund tree. They have also roped in an environmental activist group, which has launched a petition calling for citizens to be authorised as guardians of urban trees.

"When I first heard that a tree next to a museum had been poisoned with herbicide and was dying, I simply couldn't believe it," says activist Choi Jin-woo.

But when he saw the ginkgo shrivelling, he "realised something this horrific could actually happen in our society".

If there's a silver lining to be found in the ginkgo's troubles, it's that the campaign to keep it alive has brought the people of Buam-dong closer together.

While spending her days garnering support, Jung would return to find home-cooked meals from her neighbours left by her door. She, in turn, made vegetable soup for neighbours she'd never met before.

As summer went by, they all watched the ginkgo's branches increasingly go bare and brown. An arborist who inspected it said it was "90% of the way toward death", Choi says.

The fate of the tree is now "in the hands of heaven", says a resigned Jung. "Perhaps all I can do is stay beside it and pray."

For weeks, around 20 residents regularly gathered in front of the tree to pray for its recovery. Some recited Whanki's essays, while a local shaman performed a "healing ritual".

Notes of well wishes fluttered against the trunk as music rang out, and the group joined hands and swayed in unison for an "elm dance", which some nature lovers and activists believe helps trees heal.

"If someone had truly understood this tree was deeply loved, they probably would not have made the decision to inject herbicide," says Kim Min-joo, who has lived in Buam-dong for more than a decade.

It recently occurred to Jung that all the days that she spent scrambling to save the ginkgo were the most active she had been since she fell ill last winter.

She had struggled to walk much and would often observe the tree from home. On better days, she strolled up to it, even hugging its jagged trunk and inhaling the earthy scent to lift her spirits.

"I felt so depressed and hopeless but those feelings disappeared. I entered a tree-like state."

She still can't walk very much, she adds, but "the tree helped bring me back out into life again. Ironically, it was because the tree became sick."

"Although it has been heartbreaking, there were also incredibly moving moments," Jung says, on reflection. "The neighbourhood came together, cared for one another, looked after each other."

As Seoul transforms into various shades of yellow with the arrival of autumn, the leaves on Buam-dong's once-prized ginkgo are a crispy brown.

The neighbourhood is still hoping for a miracle.

Because they cannot imagine an autumn in which they don't pause to admire the ginkgo at its finest, swathed in a feathery coat of gold.

articles.title: Trump takes aim at Russia's energy sector with sanctions bill
articles.summary: The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch advocate of aid for Ukraine.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has signed a sweeping sanctions bill, taking aim at Russia's economy by punishing major purchasers of its oil and gas.

The bill, passed by the US House of Representatives earlier this week, gives Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.

At Trump's behest, the bill also extends to Iran's energy and weapons sectors.

The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.

The 48-page bill, formally titled the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, includes exceptions for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and are working to lessen their dependency.

Additionally, the bill includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.

Senator Richard Blumenthal, a New York Democrat, previously described the legislation as "scorching sanctions" which would "throttle Putin's war machine".

Data from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, or CREA, shows that China accounted for 50% of Russian crude exports between December 2022 and August 2026, followed by India at 37%.

Turkey and the European Union each accounted for 5% during the same time period, although Russian energy exports to the EU have been decreasing.

Senator Graham had long sought to push the Trump administration to do more to punish Russia for the war that followed its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The bill also had the support of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who praised its passage by the House of Representatives earlier this week.

"It is symbolic that the US House of Representatives' passage of Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill took place on the night of yet another Russian attack on Ukraine involving ballistic missiles, other missiles, and drones," Zelensky wrote on Telegram on 17 September.

Graham, 71, died on 11 July of an "aortic dissection" caused by cardiovascular disease shortly after returning from a trip to Kyiv.

"He died doing the work he was born to do," Trump said at the time.

Prior to his death, he was widely considered one of Ukraine's fiercest allies on Capitol Hill, at a time when Republicans were bitterly divided over the extent of US involvement abroad and the amount of aid being given to Ukraine.

articles.title: US and Denmark reach deal over Greenland's security after Trump threats
articles.summary: Trump said the agreement will give the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland", though specifics haven't been confirmed by Danish officials.
articles.body:
The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security, resolving a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Donald Trump's threats to seize the territory by force.

Trump said the agreement would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs".

Denmark's Prime Minister said the deal "strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" but did not address specifics in the agreement that Trump mentioned in a social media post.

The deal comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes and its mineral wealth.

Trump, in a post on Truth Social, said the deal comes with "no cost to the United States" and will grant the US the ability to "to do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland".

He said it includes a rule that no US adversary can maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval".

Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen confirmed that the agreement will be signed at the United Nations General Assembly next week.

She said the agreement "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also "at the same time recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination".

She added that the deal still needs approval from legislators, and "will have to go through the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force".

Chairman of the Greenland Government Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a statement announcing the deal that it "is gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security" of Greenland, Denmark and the US.

"The agreement recognises Greenland's interests and our place in international co-operation. It is for the benefit of us all," he said.

Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the mineral-rich Danish territory, arguing that it is vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China. He even threatened military action in Greenland, prompting an outcry from Danes and other Nato countries.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called it a "historic deal" and a "huge win for the United States and the American people".

"This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland," he said in a statement.

No text of the agreement has been released. The BBC has reached out to the Danish Embassy and the White House.

However, an unnamed US State Department official outlined the deal without providing specifics.

Among the agreed provisions is one stating the deal would not expire even if Greenland became an independent country in the future.

The official added that under the deal, the US has unilateral power to build additional military structures with no approval needed from Greenland or Denmark. It includes "permanent access, basing and overflights rights," the official said.

It also bans non-Nato countries from building bases in Greenland, and "bans adversaries from making investments in Greenland that could threaten the United States".

The official added that under the current status quo, adversaries have been allowed to invest in Greenland's "sensitive sectors without investment screening".

The official specifically referenced Russia and China, saying it blocks them from deploying troops or making investments in "sensitive sectors".

Without the official text being released, it is unclear how exactly the deal differs from a 1951 agreement with Denmark, under which the US can send as many troops as it wants to Greenland.

The US already has more than 100 military personnel permanently stationed at its Pituffik base in the north-western tip of the territory.

Trump says Greenland is essential for his plan to build a Golden Dome defence system, designed to protect the US against missile attacks from Russia and China, and that European allies could co-operate in this endeavor.

The island has vast - and largely untapped - reserves of rare earth minerals, many of which are crucial for technologies including mobile phones and electric vehicles.

But that doesn’t mean the animosity toward their former head coach in Oxford has to simmer down before kickoff. As he makes his way back to Oxford on Saturday afternoon to lead his Tigers into hostile territory, it's pretty obvious that a large percentage of the fan base still holds a grudge for the way in which Lane Kiffin bolted town after Thanksgiving last year, and just two weeks before the College Football Playoff was set to begin. He's defiantly scheming, he knows what he's doing, whether that's putting Leavitt on the injury report, he's f---ing playing. He's just a scumbag." Oxford is buzzing with excitement ahead of Kiffin's return and Top-10 showdown On a beautiful, but hot, Friday afternoon in Oxford, fans flooded the historic Square located in the middle of downtown Oxford for some good eats and drinking. No matter what takes place on the field inside Vaught Hemingway Stadium on Saturday evening, LSU head coach Lane Kiffin will be at the forefront of a hostile environment. At this point, fans were expecting nothing less. And, if any one thinks different, you don't know Kiffin. Think of it as a professional wrestler drawing boos from a crowded arena. Now, think of Lane playing the role of Hulk Hogan's NWO persona. Everything is a show, and Kiffin is selling advertisement for his return to Oxford. Think about what took place earlier this week when the LSU head coach put Sam Leavitt on the initial injury report, listing him as 'doubtful', before upgrading him to 'questionable' on Thursday evening. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Ole Miss head coach Pete Golding wasn’t buying it, not for one minute. "Well, I got the text before the report went out from Lane, like 'Hey, our quarterback's out,'" Golding mentioned to Pat McAfee. "I'm like, 'Ok buddy, I bet he is.' I've been around here a lot of Wednesday’s with you man for three and half years. I said, I think our first one had 42 guys on the first ever SEC injury report on a Wednesday. "So, I was like, 'Yea man, see ya Saturday.'" There will be trash talking that takes place on Saturday that would make a standup comedian blush. Most of it will be directed at Lane Kiffin, while LSU fans will undoubtedly take some of the heat on deflection. articles.title: Panther Creek III wind farm upgrades 133 turbines for more power and reuses nearly 90% of old blade material in cement
articles.summary: US News: A wind farm in West Texas has gained additional generating capacity while giving its old turbine blades a new industrial use. Panther Creek III, which.
articles.body: A wind farm in West Texas has gained additional generating capacity while giving its old turbine blades a new industrial use. Panther Creek III, which began operating in 2009 with 133 turbines, underwent a repowering project with longer blades and upgraded gearboxes. The work raised the wind farm’s capacity to 215 MW and was designed to increase annual electricity production from the existing turbines. At the same time, the blades removed during the upgrade were processed for use in cement production. Nearly 90% of the blade material by weight was set to be reused as engineered material for cement manufacturing.Panther Creek III capacity rises to 215 MWAccording to an RWE official press release, the changes increased Panther Creek III’s installed capacity to 215 MW. Veolia North America, which is involved in processing the removed blades, said the increase was achieved by replacing the existing blades with longer versions and upgrading the turbine gearboxes. The project therefore increased the output potential of the existing 133-turbine site without adding another set of turbines to the wind farm.RWE said the refurbishment would increase annual production across all 133 wind turbine generators. The company also described the project as a way of capturing improvements in turbine efficiency while extending the facility’s lifetime. At the time of its April 2021 announcement, RWE expected erection and commissioning of the repowering work to be completed in the third quarter of 2021.Old turbine blades reused in cement productionThe repowering also created a disposal challenge: what to do with the blades removed from the 133 turbines. Under GE Renewable Energy’s blade recycling agreement with Veolia North America, the old blades were processed for use in cement production. RWE said Veolia would use a cement-kiln co-processing technology, allowing the blade material to serve as a raw material in cement manufacturing.Veolia said the process involved the removed blades rather than sending them to landfill. Nearly 90% of the blade material by weight was expected to be reused as engineered material for cement production. Veolia also said the process could help reduce greenhouse-gas emissions associated with cement manufacturing, making the blade-repurposing operation part of the wider effort to deal with composite wind-turbine materials at the end of their original use.Panther Creek III upgrades 133 turbinesThe Panther Creek III project brought together two aspects of wind-farm repowering: increasing the productivity of an existing installation and finding a use for components removed during the upgrade. RWE’s announcement said the longer blades and upgraded gearboxes would improve the performance of the 133 turbines, while the removed blades would enter Veolia’s cement-kiln processing system.The project followed RWE’s earlier repowering work at Panther Creek I and Panther Creek II, which together involved 172 wind turbines and were repowered in the third quarter of 2019. Panther Creek III therefore became the third RWE repowering project carried out with GE Renewable Energy at the three-phase West Texas wind complex. Its move to 215 MW showed how existing wind infrastructure could be upgraded for additional generating capacity while the removed blade material was redirected towards another industrial use.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Presumption of guilt doesn't make prosecution case 'gospel truth': SC
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: In a judgment that will impact as many as nine penal laws, Supreme Court has ruled that the stringent provisions of Protection of Children .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a judgment that will impact as many as nine penal laws, Supreme Court has ruled that the stringent provisions of Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (Pocso) Act providing for presumption of guilt of the accused must not persuade trial courts to believe the prosecution's case to be the "gospel truth".A bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and N V Anjaria gave this ruling while setting aside concurrent judgments of a Delhi court and Delhi HC convicting a man, whom a woman had falsely accused of sexually assaulting her minor daughter in a Kalkaji slum in south Delhi in 2015. It said the accusation was part of a long-standing feud over water the woman had with him.The bench said both the trial court and HC appeared to have been swayed by the presumption of guilt provision in Pocso Act and overlooked glaring discrepancies and loopholes in the mother's testimony despite these being highlighted by the accused during cross-examination. Writing the judgment, Justice Anjaria said presumption of guilt in Pocso Act did not operate to eliminate evidence standing in favour of the accused.The statutory presumptions cannot be read to mean that the prosecution version is liable to be treated as gospel truth in every case," he said.The presumptive provision cannot unburden courts from "discharging their essential duty to analyse the evidence on record in light of the features emerging in a particular case", he added.This ruling will potentially impact provisions of presumption of guilt against the accused, or casting reverse burden on them, in eight other laws - Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, Prevention of Corruption Act, Wild Life (Protection) Act, Essential Commodities Act, Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, Customs Act, Foreign Exchange Management Act, and Negotiable Instruments Act, which were specifically mentioned in the 42-page judgment.Justices Mishra and Anjaria said, "The court should not mechanically accept the ipse dixit of the prosecution riding on the provisions regarding presumption of guilt to give a stamp of approval to every prosecution even if they are absurd or improbable in its story."It said the provision, or the rule of reverse burden requiring the accused to prove his innocence, did not change the rule of standard of proof as normally applied in criminal cases.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents
articles.summary: Increasingly frequent and ferocious attacks on the Ukrainian capital have left many on edge.
articles.body:
For much of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Daria was not afraid of the shelling.

Even on nights of heavy bombardment, the 27-year-old could sleep through the explosions in her apartment in Kyiv. Like many Ukrainians, she relied on the "two-wall rule": staying safe by keeping two walls between herself and the outside world.

In recent months, Russia has scaled up the intensity and frequency of its attacks against the Ukrainian capital.

In the first 10 days of July alone, the Russians launched dozens of ballistic missiles in three major attacks, killing nearly 60 civilians, according to official figures. Similar large scale attacks took place in August and September.

A BBC Verify analysis of government figures found Kyiv is now suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

It was during an attack one night in May that Daria realised she no longer felt safe in her home.

She and her boyfriend were in the corridor of their ninth-floor apartment, watching a boxing match, as explosions went off around them, the blast waves causing the windows to repeatedly slam open and shut.

When the fight ended, "there was no longer anything to distract me," Daria says. "That's when I realised I was really scared."

At first, she thought she would start using a nearby bomb shelter during attacks.

But in June, when a young mother was killed running to a shelter in Kyiv, Daria decided she needed to leave the city altogether.

She returned to her family's country house, 30km (18.6 miles) away in Romankiv, and now spends a total of four hours a day commuting to and from Kyiv, where she works in the defence sector.

Residents in Kyiv who say they had got used to Russia's missile and drone strikes have told the BBC World Service the renewed intensity of the attacks is making them rethink how they live their lives.

Previously, Ukraine's air-defence network and military intelligence gave residents a degree of predictability. Large-scale attacks could often be detected in advance, allowing people to spend the night in shelters, leave the city or take other precautions. But since the summer, Russia has changed its tactics.

It has relied less on aircraft, whose movements can be spotted ahead of time, and more on ballistic missiles that travel at tremendous speed and provide little warning. Air-raid alerts sometimes begin only moments before impact, or even simultaneously with the first explosions.

Daria can see her nearest shelter from the window of her apartment, which she still rents. Even so, it takes around 10 minutes to reach it. During a ballistic attack, she might have just four minutes' warning or less, she says.

She decided to leave Kyiv in June after holidaying abroad this summer and seeing people living "normal" lives. Since then, she has only spent one night in Kyiv.

Yet, for many, leaving is not an option.

Sixty-two-year-old Olha Vlasova lives on the seventh floor of a high-rise apartment block with her 98-year-old mother, Nadia Tsybina.

Despite her age, Nadia remains intensely engaged with the world.

From her bed she follows events in Ukraine and abroad, discussing everything from US President Donald Trump's policies, to anti-corruption protests in Kyiv, and the Epstein files.

She's also learned that she can often tell, simply by listening, whether a Russian missile or drone has been intercepted or has reached its target.

This summer, she says she has heard fewer interceptions.

"It's upsetting when there's nothing to shoot them down with," Nadia says. "I can hear them firing with whatever they've got, rifles, machine guns."

With Nadia confined to her bed, she and Olha cannot go to a shelter, however serious an attack is. Instead, as soon as an air-raid siren sounds, Olha covers her mother with a blanket, pushes a mattress into their window frame, and then hides in a wardrobe which puts two walls between her and outside.

Nadia places a pillow over her head to protect her face from flying glass.

Once in her wardrobe, Olha will often stay awake watching the news all night.

"They come in, they bomb us," Nadia says. "You haven't even had time to fall asleep, and there's another alert. They come again, they shoot them down again. And it goes on all night.

"People don't sleep, and then they walk around like zombies."

An increase in daytime attacks means life in Kyiv is now interrupted by air raid sirens day and night.

At the beginning of September, when children returned to school after the summer break, there were dozens of air raid alerts, followed by explosions and fires.

According to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, two children were injured in attacks on 31 August.

As a result, many children stayed at home, while others spent hours in the basements of schools and kindergartens.

When the sirens sound, it also affects businesses and transport. Shopping centres close and above-ground metro stations suspend operations, often severing public transport links between Kyiv's Left and Right Banks, on either side of the Dnieper River, for hours at a time.

New metro operating rules during air raid alerts are being introduced in an attempt to improve the situation.

For Olha, it has meant seeing less of her eight-year-old granddaughter, who lives on the other side of the city.

She knows if her granddaughter comes to visit, she risks struggling to return home. When metro services stop running, expensive cab journeys are Olha's only option. Crossing the river can cost as much as 1,000 hryvnias ($22, £16.6), she says, just under one-eighth of Ukraine's monthly minimum wage.

The experience has left her frustrated with what she sees as hesitation by some of Ukraine's foreign partners to provide additional air-defence missiles.

President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly appealed to allies for additional air-defence systems and interceptor missiles.

"They [Ukraine's allies] wait, thinking: 'What if we get attacked?'" Olha says. "It's like refusing to give medicine to a cancer patient because you're saying, 'What if I get sick one day?' Well, maybe you won't. Give it away before it expires."

In another part of the city, mother-of-two Natalia Bushkovska each night rehearses three different plans.

Plan A is to spread bedding in the hallway behind two interior walls; Plan B is to move the family into the building's shared corridor; and Plan C is to head for the basement.

Even there, she admits, she does not feel entirely safe.

"I keep a backpack with essential items," says Natalia, 37. "There's a tourniquet for severe bleeding. I also keep a whistle, just in case.

"If the worst happens, rescuers will be able to find us under the rubble."

Her nine-year-old daughter has her own emergency bag containing toys, lip balm and a tourniquet. Like her 12-year-old brother, she learned how to use a tourniquet through first-aid training.

Natalia says the constant attacks are exhausting.

While her son often sleeps through them, she and her daughter wake up almost every time.

"Because of the attacks, I don't get enough sleep," she says. "Now, in the fifth year of the war, I find it increasingly difficult to bounce back after nights like these."

The growing intensity of the strikes, she says, is taking a psychological toll across the city.

"People are exhausted. They don't have enough time to recover."

On Thursday 17 September, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. According to Mayor Vitali Klitschko, 20 people were injured in the attack. Among the wounded were two children, aged 10 and 12.

articles.title: Tata Sons: India's corporate crown braces for upheaval amid boardroom revolt
articles.summary: The Tata boardroom battle has intensified over a re-appointment of its chairman and a diktat to go public.
articles.body:
This week, the board of Tata Sons - one of India's oldest conglomerates and owner of iconic British brands such as Jaguar Land Rover and Tetley Tea - defied its largest shareholder, Tata Trusts, by reappointing N Chandrasekaran as chairman and backing a public listing of the holding company.

Tata Trusts, which owns 66% of Tata Sons called the decision "illegal" under its articles of association and also opposed the listing, setting the stage for a period of prolonged upheaval and possibly a protracted legal drama at Bombay House, the headquarters of the 158-year-old company.

For the Tatas, who are no strangers to boardroom battles , a cloud of uncertainty now prevails at multiple levels.

The resolution to reappoint Chandrasekharan, while approved by the board, could be defeated at the company's Annual General Meeting as Tata Trusts is likely to vote against it, putting a question mark over his future.

The meeting has to take place before 31 December as per reports, after the previous one was adjourned for lack of quorum, but no new date has yet been announced.

"The Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) of the Board of Tata Sons which reappointed him has no power to take this decision. They can only make a recommendation. Also, their decision flies against the governance code of the company that requires executives to step down from active roles at 65. These are serious lapses," Nitin Potdar, a prominent Mumbai-based corporate lawyer told the BBC.

Chandrasekharan, who got a five-year extension, will turn 65 in 2028.

Tata Group stocks first soared and then crashed as the tensions mounted, reflecting hope and uncertainty about leadership and business continuity amid several high-stakes but loss-making bets by Chandrasekharan in sectors like semiconductors and airlines.

But beyond the leadership tussle, the bigger question to contend with is the group's public listing, "which now looks increasingly inevitable", Nirmalya Kumar, who previously headed strategy at Tata Sons, told the BBC.

In 2022, India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), classified Tata Sons as an "upper layer non-banking financial company" because of its systemic importance and investment activities. This created a listing obligation on the group.

Tata Sons sought to get out of this classification by repaying their debt and arguing that they do not borrow directly from the public markets.

But after sitting on its application for over two years, the RBI rejected the company's bid to get out of the framework earlier this month, pushing the group closer to a stock market debut.

In a statement, Tata Trusts reiterated its long-held opposition to going public and said "all available options and not a listing alone" are being explored even though its trustees are no longer unanimous in their position on the matter.

Potdar says the regulator has no power to force any company to go public and the issue will almost certainly be legally challenged by Tata Trusts.

The RBI meanwhile has pre-emptively approached the courts seeking to be heard first in any matter related to the ‌listing.

The issue has sharply divided opinion among corporate pundits.

Many in the group, including the late Ratan Tata and veteran director NA Soonawala, have long argued strongly for keeping the group private.

A publicly held Tata Sons could significantly reduce the control and special rights the Tata Trusts wield over the group.

They say the Tatas have a unique operating structure where the majority shareholder is a charity which uses dividends received from commercial arms to fund hospitals, universities and research.

A listing, they say, will destroy its character by making it accountable to outside shareholders whose focus would be financial returns.

"A new group of shareholders might say, 'Don't declare dividends; we need to reinvest this money in the companies.' What happens then? The first casualty will be the hospitals they run," said Potdar.

Opponents of the initial public offering (IPO) also worry that bringing in public investors will weaken the group's internal support function to rescue distressed businesses and expose the company to quarterly performance pressures.

Moreover the timing is another crucial factor.

"The group currently faces large financial commitments from recently formed subsidiary companies, including Air India, investments in long gestation projects, and losses in newer ventures," Soonawala wrote in a piece for Times of India.

"The current situation in the case of Air India would be an acid test. All these would need to be disclosed fully in an IPO prospectus. Consolidated financial statements – reflecting subsidiary losses and borrowings – may not present an especially attractive picture to sophisticated investors, pointing to wrong timing for an IPO at the present time."

Many, including Potdar, also argue that globally , industrial foundations are being protected as sources of patient capital - money that can be committed for years to fund long-gestation projects and social goals. By forcing the Tatas to list, India is going the other way.

But supporters of a listing say it would bring much-needed transparency and accountability to a group that is systemically important to India.

"There should be tougher scrutiny of their capital-allocation decisions being so central to the Indian business ecosystem. Everybody wants complete control over their empire and the freedom to take capricious decisions, but that is not a good thing for the organisation," said Kumar.

Collectively, listed Tata companies including Tata Motors and TCS have a market capitalisation of more than $260bn and influence over 17.7 million retail shareholders, pension funds, insurers and mutual funds, investment advisory firm InGovern said.

"[It] cannot reasonably remain outside the governance and transparency expectations increasingly associated with systemically important financial and industrial conglomerates," the report added.

It also argued that shareholders of listed Tata companies are indirectly affected by Tata Sons' decisions, even though they have no direct voting rights in the holding company.

Moreover, given that the Tatas have recently made several high stakes global bets, making iPhones for Apple, partnering with Nvidia on artificial intelligence and Boeing, Airbus and Singapore Airlines on aerospace and aviation, InGovern says, a "flexible and transparent capital structure increasingly important".

Some experts say a listing may now be the only way to ease increasingly fractious relations between the board and shareholders - tensions that are hurting not just the group, but India more broadly.

Tata Trusts hold controlling economic interest and veto rights over Tata Sons board appointments and capital allocation decisions above a certain threshold.

It's hard to imagine the latter can function effectively on crucial issues of national interest - such as turning around Air India or raising funds to pay off a large minority shareholder like the SP Group which is in urgent need of cash to avert a potentially ruinous default - if it can no longer see eye to eye with its biggest shareholder.

Whatever happens on the listing front, experts say India's biggest trophy asset is entering totally uncharted territory. As Kumar suspects, "a new twist" can be expected every week.

articles.title: Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of launching 26 strikes in 24 hours
articles.summary: The war in Yemen intensifies with mounting clashes and reciprocal attacks between Saudi forces and the Houthis.
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthi rebels have said Saudi Arabia carried out 26 strikes against areas under the group’s control in the past 24 hours, as the two sides continue trading attacks amid an escalating war in Yemen, according to the AFP news agency.

On Friday, the group claimed Saudi strikes on Houthi-held territory had reached 300 over the past week alone, hitting positions across the areas it controls, AFP reported.

Yemen’s government, backed by Saudi Arabia, said on Friday its forces had killed 30 Houthi rebels and wounded more than 60 in clashes in the al-Wazi’iyah district of Taiz province, one of several fronts where combat has picked up this week.

The exchange has come on the heels of a widening escalation of fighting in Yemen between the government’s military and the Houthi fighters.

Tens of thousands marched through Sanaa on Friday in a show of support for the Iran-backed Houthis and against Saudi Arabia, as the rebels press gains that have brought large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, under their control.

Earlier this week, the intensifying attacks between the Yemeni government and the Houthi rebels killed at least five people, including three children, according to reports from both sides.

Saudi Arabia said one person was killed in the Taif governorate after a Houthi drone was intercepted, while Houthi-linked media reported deaths from Saudi strikes in Taiz and the town of Abs.

The escalation has drawn in Washington, though reluctantly.

US officials met Houthi representatives at the US embassy in the Omani capital, Muscat, over the weekend after the group’s rapid territorial gains raised concern over shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, a vital corridor for global trade.

The Houthis reportedly assured Washington that vessels not linked to Saudi Arabia would not be targeted.

Despite appeals from Riyadh for US President Donald Trump to strike the Houthis directly, Washington has so far held back, wary of opening a new front while still fighting a costly war with Iran.

Meanwhile, European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Friday the bloc’s Red Sea naval mission, Operation Aspides, had raised its alert level as the situation in the region worsened, the Reuters news agency reported.

“Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are unacceptable and sabotage the global economy,” Kallas said in a post on X.

She added that she had spoken with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud about diplomatic efforts to end the fighting in Yemen and restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: An American found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and hopes others do too
articles.summary: Mary Timby flew to Ireland on a whim last year and met her boyfriend at a matchmaking festival.
articles.body:
Mary Timby was fed up with dating apps when she booked a trip to Ireland on a whim last summer - from the comfort of her Colorado couch.

The spur-of-the-moment trip was unlike her: Timby, 39, is a self-described "total planner".

But she'd always wanted to visit Ireland, and she found herself exhausted by the local dating scene while navigating a career transition. And then she remembered a few throwaway lines from a comedy series about a matchmaking festival in Ireland.

So she looked it up - and not only was the Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival real, it was also taking place during the entire month of September, when she was scheduled to visit.

Now, a little more than a year later, Timby is reaping the benefits of that uncharacteristic last-minute decision: She's become a viral star. She's found love with an Irishman she met at a pub called The Matchmaker. And she's even started a new business venture - bringing others to Lisdoonvarna who hope to follow in her footsteps.

"It's really about enjoying County Clare, enjoying the festival, and, if you meet someone, you do - and that's what happened with us," says Timby, smiling at her partner, Jason Mangan, sitting beside her.

They're speaking from the windswept coastal cottage they rented together for the summer in his native County Clare - about 20 miles (32 km) southwest of Lisdoonvarna, the site of their first fortuitous meeting.

From the outset, Timby's inaugural Ireland trip seemed to take on a life of its own.

She filmed a short video on the plane before her flight took off, telling her approximately 300 TikTok followers that she was heading on an off-the-cuff trip to an Irish matchmaking festival - and didn't "know what's going to happen".

Timby then "turned my phone on airplane mode, then spent about eight hours on the flight (and) woke up at Shannon Airport," she says.

When she turned on her phone, "it was blowing up".

A group of friends had texted her. "They said, 'Mary, your video is going viral,'" she says. "I didn't even have notifications on for social media."

She rented a manual transmission car - horrified to find the gear stick on the left side of the driver's seat - and set off through County Clare to her accommodation at an Irish family's home.

Then she headed to Lisdoonvarna, where she saw firsthand that the festival is a whole-town, month-long celebration of conversation and dancing, rather than a line of singles waiting to be set up by a sage local matchmaker.

That's changed since the festival's origins 170 years ago, when bachelor farmers and moneyed visitors would flock to the spa town of Lisdoonvarna to bathe in its mineral-rich waters and socialise. Generations of matchmakers would ply their trade to set up successful marriages, and word spread. Now, while the town's year-round residents number fewer than 1,000, that number swells up to 80,000 each September as revellers descend upon Lisdoonvarna from around the world.

Third-generation matchmaker Willie Daly still holds court at his nearby home and at festival events, and Timby even visited him during her trip - when he put her on the phone to random men whose accents she struggled to understand.

But the real magic of contemporary Lisdoonvarna lies in the town's overflowing streets and pubs - as Timby soon found out.

Her first night in town was "a little slow," she admits - and Timby was tired and jet-lagged. She retired to her room and spent the next day sightseeing, but the Irish woman running her accommodation convinced her to try Lisdoonvarna again that night.

"My AirBnB host said, 'You should go back tonight, because I heard that the younger folks come out at night,'" laughs Timby.

So she did - and found herself dancing and drinking pints at The Matchmaker Bar in the centre of town. That's when a "handsome Irishman" approached her.

"I went over and introduced myself, and... conversation just flowed," says Mangan, 38, from Ennis, County Clare, about 22 miles southeast of Lisdoonvarna. He'd been to the festival before and was well-acquainted with its cultural significance, remembering his grandparents making the journey decades earlier for the dancing.

"Unfortunately, I didn't have much time on my hands, because I was turning back to Ennis," says Mangan, designated driver that night for a group of friends. "So I got her name, and I said, 'Oh, sure, I might see you around.'

"It was a very short interaction, to be honest with you."

He didn't leave it at that, though; Mangan found Timby on Instagram and followed up with a message inviting her out.

"It was short and sweet, and it was really genuine, too," says Timby - and she took him up on the offer.

What followed was a series of whirlwind dates - lunches, dinners, sightseeing and shopping trips. Timby extended her time in Ireland and documented much of it for her newfound following - but she didn't reveal anything about her new beau. They wanted to save the burgeoning romance for themselves.

When Timby eventually had to fly home, there were "tears at the airport" - but they decided to keep the relationship going.

"It was very tough to say goodbye," Timby says. "It was very tough to start a long-distance relationship, but it ended up being a really good opportunity for us to sort of slow things down a bit."

They kept talking daily, Mangan impatiently waiting for Timby to wake up seven hours behind him in Colorado. She flew back to Ireland again, then he made his first trip to America for Thanksgiving 2025. Timby returned to Ireland at Christmas and met his family, and after that, they decided to make her boyfriend's big social media reveal.

"We thought, this is something we already know we want to invest in... we were ready to share," Timby says. "So New Year's Eve, we shared a photo of him, and people were just over-the-moon excited."

The pair watched their following grow, drawing interest from Irish cafes and tourist destinations to the local Gaelic sports club in Colorado. Their story also caught the attention of Lisdoonvarna locals, who approached Timby - a communications consultant - about being an ambassador for the festival.

"So I said: Sign me up," Timby laughs. "I love the festival. It brought me Jay."

Timby's been inundated with messages from lovelorn followers hoping to replicate her matchmaking success.

"I heard from many of my followers... groups of people wanting to go to the festival but not having anyone to go with" or "not knowing what to do," Timby says. "I really listened to that, and I also wanted to be mindful of the fact that I love Ireland.

"I'm so excited to showcase County Clare and all the amazing things that the west coast of Ireland has, but I'm also not a tour operator."

So she partnered with a company called Met Through Friends, which organises and encourages real-life meetups for people looking for love. They released an interest form for a trip, expecting "80 to 100 responses." They received 560.

The first group of eight will make the trip later this month, with Timby's Irish boyfriend consulting on the itinerary.

"You can go on all these apps, swipe left, swipe right, but it's not actually going out and making a connection with someone and experiencing a small little town in Ireland, experiencing the culture," says Mangan.

"It's a once-in-a-lifetime experience... you never know."

Timby, smiling at her boyfriend of one year, agrees.

"I echo everything Jay just said," she says. "Put your phone down and put yourselves out there, and good things will come."
